learn.hook: Two batters both average 50. One scores 48, 50, 52 every match; the other scores 0, 100, 0, 100. Same mean — very different reliability. That difference is dispersion.
points: Statistics collects, organises and interprets data. Mean, median and mode (from Class 10) are measures of central tendency: they give a typical value.
Data sets with the same mean can be spread very differently, so we also need measures of dispersion.
Dispersion is the scatter (variability) of observations about a central value.
Measures of dispersion: range, quartile deviation, mean deviation and standard deviation (with variance).
Range = maximum value − minimum value. It is quick but uses only the two extreme values.

topics.title: Grouped median, M.D. about the median, and limitations

learn.hook: For a big class table, the median isn't a value you can just spot — it's found with a formula, and then you measure spread around it.
points: Median of grouped data: find N/2, locate the median class (first cumulative frequency ≥ N/2).
Median = l + [(N/2 − C)/f] × h, where l = lower limit of the median class, C = cumulative frequency before it, f = its frequency, h = class width.
M.D. about the median = (1/N) Σ fᵢ|xᵢ − M|, using class marks xᵢ.
Limitations of M.D.: absolute values are awkward to handle algebraically; it is not well suited to further statistical work.
Also, if the data are very variable, the median is not a good representative, and the sum of absolute deviations about the mean is larger than about the median, so the choice of centre matters.

topics.title: Variance and standard deviation for raw data

learn.hook: Squaring deviations removes the sign problem AND gives a measure with beautiful algebra. That's why standard deviation rules statistics.
points: Squaring deviations makes them non-negative and avoids absolute values. Variance σ² = (1/n) Σ (xᵢ − x̄)², the mean of squared deviations.
Standard deviation σ = +√(variance). It has the same units as the data.
Shortcut: σ² = (1/n)Σxᵢ² − (x̄)² = [nΣxᵢ² − (Σxᵢ)²]/n².
σ = 0 exactly when all observations are equal.

learn.hook: A teacher discovers one mark was entered as 15 instead of 25. Do you redo everything? No — fix the sums Σx and Σx², and recompute in a minute.
points: First n natural numbers: mean (n + 1)/2, variance (n² − 1)/12. Multiples k, 2k, …, nk: mean k(n + 1)/2, variance k²(n² − 1)/12.
Missing observations: use Σx = n x̄ and Σx² = n(σ² + x̄²) to form equations.
Adding a constant c to every value: mean increases by c, variance unchanged. Multiplying by k: mean × k, variance × k², SD × |k|.
Correcting errors: correct Σx and Σx² (subtract the wrong value, add the right one), then recompute x̄ and σ² = Σx²/n − x̄².
Always keep n the same unless observations are actually added or removed.

revise.summary: The first n natural numbers have mean (n + 1)/2 and variance (n² − 1)/12. Adding c shifts the mean but not the variance; multiplying by k multiplies the mean by k and the variance by k². To correct errors, fix Σx and Σx², then recompute.
focus: Use mean and variance formulas for 1, 2, …, n and their multiples
Find missing observations from given mean and variance
Apply the effect of adding or multiplying by a constant
Correct a wrongly read value in Σx and Σx²
remember: 1, 2, …, n: mean (n + 1)/2, variance (n² − 1)/12
Σx = n x̄ and Σx² = n(σ² + x̄²)
Add c: mean + c, variance same; multiply by k: mean × k, variance × k², SD × |k|
traps: Multiplying by k multiplies the variance by k², not by k
When correcting, remove the wrong value's square from Σx² and add the right one's square
